title: HMRC late payment interest rises to 8% from 24 November 2026
summary: The Bank of England raised base rate to 4.00%, so HMRC's interest on late tax goes up to 8% a year. Here is what it means for anyone with a tax bill due on 31 January.
body:
On 5 November 2026 the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75% to 4.00%. HMRC's interest rates are set by law and follow base rate, so the interest HMRC charges on late tax is going up.

What is changing

  • Late payment interest is set at base rate plus 4%. With base rate at 4.00%, that means 8% a year, up from 7.75%.
  • Repayment interest, which HMRC pays when you have overpaid, is base rate minus 1%, so it rises to 3%.
  • The new rates apply from 24 November 2026 for most taxes, including Self Assessment, and from 16 November 2026 for companies paying corporation tax by quarterly instalments.

Why it matters now

The Self Assessment deadline is 31 January 2027. That is the date to file your 2025 to 2026 tax return and pay any tax owed, plus your first payment on account for 2026 to 2027 if one applies. Interest runs on any amount not paid by the due date, day by day, until it is paid. Late payment penalties are charged on top of interest.

At 8%, an unpaid bill of £5,000 builds up roughly £33 of interest a month. It is not a disaster, but it adds up quickly when a bill is left for a few months, and interest is not tax deductible for individuals.

What I would do

  • File early. Filing in December does not mean paying in December, but it tells you the exact figure while there is still time to plan for it.
  • Check your payments on account. If your income has fallen, you may be able to reduce them. If it has risen, budget for a higher balancing payment.
  • Talk to HMRC before the deadline if you cannot pay. A Time to Pay arrangement can spread the bill, although interest still runs on the unpaid amount.
  • Companies: if your company pays corporation tax by quarterly instalments, the higher rate already applies from 16 November.
